slides.title: Linked Lists
slides.main: A list is cheap to rearrange but costly at answering "what is at number N".

captions: Array: elements in a row, instant reads, costly rearranging
List: nodes scattered around memory, a mirror image
Each node knows only the next one: all list properties follow
Reversal, cycle, merge, ring queue: twenty exercises

body.text: Twenty exercises: singly and doubly linked lists, ring queue, queue of two stacks.

slides.title: Node and reference
slides.sub: The head is the only entry point
slides.main: Access by index in a list is O(n): the address is written nowhere.

captions: A node is a value and a reference to the next; the last reference is empty
The whole list is a reference to the first node, the head
Traversal: process the node, follow the reference; linear time
Element number 3 can't be taken directly: follow the references. Access by index is O(n)

frames.text: while cur is not empty: cur = cur.next
3 hops to the element with index 3

slides.title: Insertion and deletion
slides.sub: The order of assignments is critical
slides.main: Before changing a reference, save what it pointed to.

captions: Insert X after B: two references to reassign
B → X first: the old tail C is remembered by no one and is lost
First X → C (saved the tail), then B → X
Two or three operations, no shifting: constant time

frames.text: O(1) if you are already standing at B

slides.title: Sentinel node
slides.main: A sentinel before the head removes the branching: every node has a previous one.

captions: Deleting from the middle is easy; but what if it's the head itself?
The head has no previous node, so the code branches on a separate condition
A sentinel is a dummy before the real head: every node now has a previous one
The same line for the head, the middle and the tail

slides.title: List reversal
slides.main: One pass, O(1) memory: switch references, no new nodes.

captions: Three variables: prev, cur and next, remember the rest so it isn't lost
The first node now points to prev (empty): it became the tail
The second node points back, to the first
The third points to the second; cur reached the end, prev is the new head
One pass, O(n) time and O(1) memory: only references switched

slides.title: Fast and slow
slides.main: When fast is at the end, slow is in the middle, no need to count the length.

captions: Two pointers from the head: slow by one step, fast by two
Fast moved to the second node, slow to the second from the head
Fast is almost at the end
Fast reached the end, slow is exactly in the middle, no length counting

slides.title: Cycle start
slides.main: After they meet, one pointer goes to the head, both step by one: they meet at the cycle start.

captions: A tail of two nodes, then a circle: fast never reaches emptiness
Inside the circle fast gains a step per tick on slow: they met
From the meeting point to the cycle start is as many steps as from the head
One pointer to the head, both by one step: met exactly at the cycle start

frames.text: p1 = head, both by one step

slides.title: Merge and sort
slides.main: Merge in O(n + m) with no new nodes; merge sort is O(n log n) with almost no memory.

captions: Two sorted lists; build the result by attaching the smaller head
1 < 2: first goes to the result, advance a
2 and 3 are less than 4: they move to the result from the second list
4 < 8: again from the first
First list ended: attach the second's tail whole; no new nodes

slides.title: Doubly linked list
slides.main: A node deletes itself in O(1): the neighbors know each other.

captions: Each node has two references: to the next and to the previous
We want to delete B, and all we hold is B itself
Left and right neighbors become neighbors of each other; no search for the previous
Two operations: O(1). The price is an extra reference per node

slides.title: Queue and deque
slides.main: Queue and deque on a doubly linked list with sentinels: O(1) at both ends.

captions: Two sentinels, at the start and at the end: even an empty list looks the same
Add to the tail: insert before the right sentinel, O(1), no special cases
Remove from the head: delete the node after the left sentinel, O(1)
Deque: both ends are cheap; eviction caches are built on the same frame

slides.title: Ring buffer
slides.sub: A queue on a fixed-length array
slides.main: Index around the circle: (i + 1) % n; a counter tells empty from full.

captions: An array of six cells and two indexes: head and tail
Three elements written, the tail moved forward
Two removed, the head moved, no memory copied
The tail reached the edge and wrapped to the start: index = (index + 1) % 6
Head equals tail: empty or full? We need a counter of occupied slots

slides.title: Queue from two stacks
slides.main: Each element is poured once: removal is amortized O(1).

captions: New elements go onto the first stack: 1, 2, 3, 4, the oldest at the bottom
The second is empty, so pour: the order reverses, the oldest ends up on top
Remove from the second stack: the oldest comes out first, this is a queue
Each element is poured at most once: removal is amortized constant

frames.text: one move per element → amortized O(1)

slides.title: List or array
slides.main: In practice an array often wins even where the list promises victory.

captions: Traversal of all elements: the array has the cache, the list jumps around memory (illustrative)
Insert in the middle: the list must first get there, the array quickly shifts
Lists live in narrow roles, not as general-purpose collections

slides.title: Summary and practice
slides.main: References, special cases, cycles: draw the arrows on paper.

captions: Losing a reference: before redirecting a pointer, save what it pointed to
Empty list, one element, head and tail: check explicitly with tests
A sentinel node removes a whole class of bugs
From the length of a list to a queue with a constant-time minimum
